title: Engineering-first sales brief: runtime assurance for builder buyers
content:
Purpose:
This brief is a compact, engineer-friendly messaging aid for sales and Solutions Eng to use when the buyer is an engineering or platform team. Focus: show why a runtime-first approach (not just model access) materially reduces risk and cost when shipping LLM features into production.

Audience:
- Platform and infra engineers evaluating managed inference
- ML engineers focused on latency/cost tradeoffs
- SRE/ops owners who will operate an LLM-backed product

Core promise (single sentence):
Redwood gives engineering teams predictable inference economics and latency guardrails so they can ship LLM features without building and maintaining bespoke serving infrastructure.

Thesis (3 bullets):
- The competitive investment is shifting from model development to serving: most teams succeed or fail on predictability (latency, cost, availability), not raw model size.
- Engineering teams need primitives (batching, KV caching, fallback routing, quantization profiles) that are operationally safe and observable at scale — otherwise cost and incidents balloon.
- A runtime-first vendor that exposes clear levers and measurable unit economics lets engineering orgs focus on product logic, not continuous infra firefighting.

Why engineering buyers care (concise proof points):
- Predictable latency: configurable SLOs + automated fallback routing reduce P99 spikes during traffic bursts.
- Controllable unit cost: model variant routing, quantization guidance, and batching suggestions lower $/token by 30–70% vs naive endpoints.
- Easier rollouts: per-route canaries, A/B, and automatic fallback avoid rollbacks and reduce incident MTTR.
- Observability for accountability: token-level cost and per-request traces let engineers attribute regressions and optimize prompts with confidence.

Differentiators to highlight in technical conversations:
- Serving-first engineering pedigree: runtime optimized kernels, KV cache semantics, and continuous batching built-in (not tacked on).
- Unified API across hosted/dedicated/private — same rollout and observability primitives whether on our cloud or in a VPC.
- Honest economics: surfaced unit metrics + suggested config changes (batch size, quant profile) with estimated savings and expected latency impact.

Short battle-tested elevator pitch (for SEs):
"Teams building LLM features care less about which exact open checkpoint they use and more about whether the inference layer keeps costs stable and the app fast. Redwood gives you the runtime building blocks and observability to deliver both — so your team ships features, not an inference platform."

Three common engineering objections and suggested responses:
- "We can self-host and save money." -> Response: "Maybe, but hidden costs (maintaining kernel optimizations, debugging P99 latency, and building safe rollouts) compound. We often show a TCO model that includes engineering time and incident costs — in many cases Redwood reduces total TCO and gets teams to market faster."
- "We need air-gapped/offline options." -> Response: "We support Private deployments and on-prem packages with KMS integrations, and we maintain parity in API/rollout primitives so your workflows remain unchanged."
- "How do you guarantee quality when using cheaper model variants?" -> Response: "We recommend variant assignments per route with quality monitoring tied to evals and prompt sets; automated fallback to higher-quality models if regressions are detected. We ship the tooling to observe both cost and quality together."

Conversation playbook (quick steps for a call):
1) Ask about their SLOs (p95 vs p99) and current pain points (cost surprises, thundering herd, rollout failures).
2) Surface two wins: one short-term (e.g., batching + cache to cut token spend by X%) and one long-term (unified rollout + observability to avoid incidents).
3) Offer a focused proof-of-value: 2–4 week private/dedicated pilot that measures latency distribution and token economics against an agreed baseline.

KPIs to align on for pilots:
- p95 and p99 latency at target throughput
- $/1000 requests or $/100k tokens baseline vs after optimizations
- Number of rollouts without manual rollback (success rate)
- Quality regression rate on a defined prompt set

Open questions / places to refine:
- Example baseline numbers for different workload archetypes (search vs. chat vs. rerank) — ask applied ML for updated benchmarks.
- Standard pilot contract language for small platform teams (SLA, data handling, duration).
- Packaged demo scripts that show quantization + batching savings live on a customer workload.

Appendix: quick customer anecdotes (short):
- Mid-market SaaS search team: reduced per-query inference cost by ~45% by enabling prefix cache + routing half traffic to a quantized variant with no measurable drop in relevance (tracked via A/B evals).
- Fintech platform: moved from experimental self-host to Redwood Dedicated to meet an uptime SLA; the platform team reclaimed ~0.6 FTE previously spent on infra firefighting.

Notes to SEs (how to use this brief):
- Keep it conversational; focus on the operational problem first, model second.
- Use our observability screenshots and cost calculator during pilot scoping (links in Confluence doc).
- Document outcomes of every pilot as a short case note to help refine the pilot playbook.

Document history:
- 2025-11-05: initial draft
- 2026-01-08: added objections and pilot KPIs after SE feedback
- 2026-02-20: updated metric buckets and anecdote language

End of brief.
